name: LED light facial

lead: An LED light facial exposes the face to specific wavelengths of light, with blue aimed at acne and red or near-infrared at skin ageing and texture, for clearer, firmer-looking skin.

Light is thought to be absorbed by mitochondria in skin cells, influencing repair and inflammation, a process called photobiomodulation. Small trials of LED treatment for facial rejuvenation exist, and Wikipedia describes the evidence as preliminary.

paras: It is used in clinics and with home masks, typically as a repeated routine over weeks.
Side effects are described as rare and mild, such as itching or redness. Photodynamic therapy, which adds a light-sensitising drug, carries more risks and is a separate procedure.

angle.text: It is used in clinics and at home for acne and skin ageing: blue light targets acne, while red and near-infrared light are used for texture. Light absorbed by skin cells is thought to reduce inflammation and boost collagen activity. Small trials show preliminary results.

lead: An LED light facial is a clinic or at-home treatment that exposes the face to light-emitting diodes at selected wavelengths (blue, red, near-infrared and others), usually for acne, skin ageing and general skin quality. It belongs to the family of low-level light therapy, or photobiomodulation.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes the proposed mechanism as light interacting with mitochondria, and describes the therapy as having rare, mild side effects, while noting that its own evidence base is flagged as needing stronger sourcing.[1] Small trials of LED treatment for facial rejuvenation exist; results for most registered studies are not available.

paras: Wikipedia lists blue light (about 415 nm) for acne, red and yellow light for collagen support and rejuvenation, and red light for hair counts in androgenetic alopecia, and notes that home masks, panels and handhelds are widely sold.[1]

Light therapy has ancient roots; Niels Finsen's lamp for skin tuberculosis in the late 1800s is treated as the start of modern phototherapy. Cosmetic LED use grew in the 1980s, and narrow-band LED work in the 1990s is linked to NASA research.[1]

Wikipedia describes LED therapy as safer than laser because the light is non-coherent and lower in intensity, with photobiomodulation side effects described as rare and mild, such as itching or redness.[1]

A 2026 study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery evaluated a new broader-spectrum near-infrared LED device for skin rejuvenation and hair growth.[2] Registered trials include a comparison of LED and laser therapy for facial rejuvenation (32 participants, completed),[3] a trial of an LED face, neck and chest mask for skin ageing and sun damage (38 participants, completed),[4] and a planned 130-person trial of an LED mask with or without a serum for photodamage.[5] Results of the registered trials were not available.
